conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you had a reaction during your barium swallow today. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I was getting the test done, and suddenly I started itching all over and couldn’t breathe well. It felt like my throat was closing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds scary. I see they gave you epinephrine and Benadryl in the ER. Was this similar to past mast cell crises you’ve had?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly like them. I’ve had maybe 25 hospitalizations for this. My allergist has a protocol—IV Benadryl, steroids, and Dilaudid for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re following that protocol. You’ve already received methylprednisolone, Benadryl, and Dilaudid. Your vitals are stabilizing, and your oxygen is good on 2 liters.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. But the chest tightness is still here. It’s usually from my esophageal spasms, not my heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your EKG is normal, and your troponins came back negative twice, so it’s unlikely to be your heart. We’ll keep managing the spasms with Dilaudid and methadone as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I can’t use nitroglycerin—it drops my blood pressure too much. IV Dilaudid works best when I’m here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’ll stick with IV pain control as needed. We also did a chest X-ray. It shows low lung volumes, but no pneumonia or fluid. That matches your history of reduced air movement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The barium test—did it show anything new?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It confirmed esophageal dysmotility—uncoordinated contractions in the lower esophagus. There’s also a small hiatal hernia, even after your prior surgery, and the barium pill held up at the junction for a few minutes before passing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That explains the pain. But why did I react during the test? I’ve had barium before without issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure. It could be the barium itself, or the procedure stress triggering your mast cells. We’ll discuss with your allergist whether to premedicate with Benadryl next time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’m just worried it’ll happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure your care team knows. For now, rest and the current meds should help. We’ll monitor you overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The itching and breathing issues are gone. Chest tightness is less, but still there when I eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Your labs this morning are stable—potassium is 4.0, and your CBC and kidney function are normal. We’ll keep you on the IV steroids for one more dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Can I switch back to my oral meds soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll transition you to oral Dilaudid and methadone. You’re also on famotidine and omeprazole for GERD, which we’ll continue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I stopped cholestyramine—didn’t help and caused bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve discontinued it in your discharge plan. We’ll also keep your other regular meds: carvedilol, aspirin, furosemide, and your RA treatments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my Humira dose? It’s due this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve confirmed it’s 40 mg subcutaneous every two weeks. You’ll get your next dose on schedule after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my thyroid? I take 25 mcg levothyroxine daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue that. Your calcium and magnesium are normal, so no supplements needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The GI team reviewed your barium swallow. They recommend follow-up to discuss managing the dysmotility and pill hold-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I avoid pills? I take so many.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily, but take them with plenty of water and stay upright. They may suggest liquid forms or crushing some, but we’ll confirm with GI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That helps. And for mast cell—should I avoid future imaging with contrast or barium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not avoid, but premedicate. We’ll recommend Benadryl and steroids before any future procedures, especially with barium or contrast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Vital signs are stable, and you’ve been eating without major issues. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have severe itching, trouble breathing, or chest tightness that doesn’t improve with your meds, go to the ER. Otherwise, follow up with your allergist and GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have my EpiPen. Should I use it if I feel a crisis starting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially if you have throat tightness or trouble breathing. Then call 911. Your protocol is clear—don’t wait if symptoms are severe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re ready to go home. Your exam is normal, and labs are stable. We’ve updated your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. All my meds are listed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, including your pain, heart, thyroid, and RA meds. We’ve also added a note about premedicating before future procedures due to your mast cell risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. I’ll follow up with my doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad we could help. Take care, and reach out if anything changes.
